name: actor
intent: Partition mutable state into isolated, addressable actors that process one protocol message in a single logical turn, so other components communicate through asynchronous messages and actor references rather than shared memory and locks.
problem: Concurrent requests need to update many independently owned entities - such as sessions, devices, orders or rooms - without races between reads and writes. Sharing that state across threads makes visibility, locking and deadlock behavior part of every call; the design decision is to give each entity one owner and one mailbox serialization point instead of another lock or concurrent collection.
context: Use when many independently mutating entities or long-lived message-driven tasks must remain consistent under concurrent access, especially when work is I/O-bound and the runtime provides cheap processes, coroutines, goroutines, virtual threads or an actor framework. It fits an addressable state machine whose lifecycle, supervision and possibly placement matter; it is not a promise of FIFO delivery, durable state or free distributed consistency.
benefits: No locks around actor state: all mutation happens in the actor's single logical thread of control, so data races on that state disappear by construction rather than by discipline.
Failure isolation: an actor that crashes does not corrupt the state of other actors, and a supervisor can restart or stop it (Erlang/OTP links and monitors, Akka supervision, CAF links and monitors).

Address-based communication hides location and topology: the same send works in-process, on another thread or across the network once the address is remote (Akka remoting, CAF network transparency, Orleans grains).

Elastic concurrency: because actors are cheap, thousands to millions of them multiplex over a few OS threads - goroutines, coroutines and Java 21 virtual threads exist to make the thread-per-actor style viable.
Single-writer ownership makes each entity's transitions easy to reason about and audit: everything that changes the state of an entity happens in one place, in message order.
Senders do not block on receivers: asynchronous send decouples producer and consumer timing, and a bounded mailbox adds explicit backpressure instead of hidden lock contention.
tradeoffs: Messages are values that are copied, moved or serialized - never shared: large payloads cost, and a synchronous request/reply (ask) reintroduces blocking, timeouts and deadlock risk (Rust makes moving a value into a channel a compile error; Worker postMessage structured-clones it).

A mailbox is a buffer with no natural bound: an unbounded one converts overload into memory growth and latency (Akka's default mailbox is unbounded), a bounded one converts it into producer blocking or dropped messages - the pattern does not choose the overflow policy for you.
One message at a time means per-actor throughput is single-threaded: a hot actor is a bottleneck and a long handler head-of-line-blocks every message behind it.
Causality leaves the call stack: a stack trace shows one actor step, so request tracing needs correlation ids and purpose-built tooling instead of a debugger backtrace.

Delivery is not part of the pattern: only messages between one sender-receiver pair are ordered (the actor model explicitly does not require M1 to arrive before M2), and nothing survives an actor or node death - designs must add idempotence, timeouts and dead-letter handling.

State lives in a runtime or process: an actor restart or process crash resets in-memory state unless the design persists it, and reentrant handlers (an await inside the handler) can interleave, invalidating invariants checked before the suspension point.
Actor state cannot be inspected from outside, so testing and debugging shift to message-level probes and TestKit-style harnesses.

participants.responsibility: Owns a piece of state and one behavior; processes one message at a time, may create other actors and send messages, and is never shared.
Buffers incoming messages for one actor; bounded or unbounded, and carries the overflow policy (block the sender, drop, or fail).
Immutable value carrying data and actor addresses; the only way one actor can affect another actor's state.
Stable, shareable handle used to send messages (pid, ActorRef, Ractor, Concurrent::Actor::Reference); decouples identity from location, activation and lifecycle.
Decides which actor runs next and on which thread or carrier (event loop, coroutine dispatcher, virtual-thread scheduler, actor_system scheduler, Akka dispatcher).
Creates and owns child actors, links or monitors them, and applies a restart, stop or escalate policy when a child fails.

use_cases: Session and connection state: one actor per chat room, WebSocket connection, game session or device twin, with the mailbox as its inbound buffer.
Per-entity consistency without locks: bank accounts, shopping carts, order aggregates and counters, where one actor per entity id serializes all mutations.
Work distribution and pipelines: supervisor/worker pools, stream-processing stages, ETL workers and task queues where messages carry the work.
Distributed systems: cluster sharding by entity id with location-transparent messaging (Akka Cluster Sharding, Orleans grains, CAF remoting) so callers never learn where an entity lives.
UI and state machines: XState actors or Model-View-Intent loops where a screen's state machine is the actor, and service tasks that own a resource (socket, timer, cache) exclusively.
Chat and messaging platforms: contact management, message routing, delivery receipts and presence at WhatsApp-scale reliability using supervision hierarchies for fault isolation.
Game servers: player session state, matchmaking pools, match logic and real-time state synchronization where one actor owns each player's turn and game phase.
Financial trading systems: order book management, position tracking and risk checks where one actor per instrument serializes all order modifications and prevents race conditions.
IoT device twins and edge computing: Cloudflare Durable Objects model where an actor at the edge owns device state, handles commands and maintains session continuity.

Named actor runtimes: Akka Typed or Pekko Typed provide typed ActorRef protocols and supervision for JVM services; Erlang/OTP gen_server provides the callback protocol and supervision-tree integration for fault-tolerant processes; Orleans virtual actors and Akka.NET provide stable identity and cluster placement when entities span a .NET deployment.

Protocol-driven domain entities: use an actor per account, order, device or game session when commands must be serialized, then add persistence or idempotent effects if a restart must not lose business state.

Rust services with stateful typed actors: Actix gives each actor its own Context and address (Addr), routes typed messages to Handler implementations, multiplexes many actors over a few Arbiter threads and restarts panicking actors via Supervisor.

Compiler-checked state isolation: Swift actors (SE-0306) make the mailbox a language construct - all access to actor-isolated state is serialized by the runtime and every cross-actor call is an await, so the no-data-race property is enforced by the compiler rather than by discipline.

Dense per-connection sessions: WhatsApp served 1-2 million concurrent Erlang client connections per server with one lightweight process per connection under OTP supervision trees - the production proof that process-per-entity can replace thread-per-connection at internet scale.
avoid_when: The state fits one lock or a concurrent collection: use a mutex, ReentrantLock, atomics, ConcurrentHashMap or a channel-guarded field; an actor adds indirection and a mailbox on top.
Simple request/response service calls: a direct function call, task or future is simpler than a mailbox round-trip with a reply address.
Bulk CPU-bound processing over shared read-only data: a data-parallel map or work-stealing pool uses the cores better than one mailbox per worker.
Strict global ordering of all messages is required: actor mailboxes order messages only per sender-receiver pair, so a sequencer or a single consumer must be added.
A framework already owns the concurrency (request-scoped web framework, reactive pipeline, database transaction): adding actors duplicates the serialization it already performs.

A single active object with method-style futures is the better fit when object-centric invocation and a caller-owned lifecycle matter more than actor addresses, supervision trees or location transparency.
A channel/CSP design is clearer when the main abstraction is a fixed communication topology or streaming pipeline and there is no long-lived addressable state owner behind each endpoint.
A thread pool or work-stealing executor is simpler for stateless, bounded jobs whose unit of scheduling is a task rather than an addressable entity with a mailbox.
anti_patterns: Actor-wrapped mutex: the actor hands out references to its own mutable state (or reads shared globals), so the no-shared-memory rule is broken and races return.
Blocking or ask-inside-handler: a handler synchronously waits for a reply from an actor that is itself waiting on it - a deadlock that appears only under load.
Unbounded mailbox under bursty load: producers are never backpressured, so overload becomes heap growth and then OOM instead of latency.
God actor: one actor (or one mailbox) handles all application work, serializing what was supposed to be concurrent.
Chatty message-per-field design: a method call is replaced by a dozen asynchronous messages, producing unreadable flows and lost causality.
Premature actorisation: wrapping sequential code in actors keeps the indirection without any concurrent access to protect.

Ask at the composition boundary only: using ask (request/response) for routine actor-to-actor communication allocates a temporary listener per call — prefer tell with forward or dedicated aggregator actors for multi-actor scatter-gather flows.
design_principles: Share nothing: only immutable values and actor addresses cross an actor boundary.
Single writer per state: exactly one actor owns each piece of mutable state.
Encapsulation: the actor's state is private and changes only through its message protocol (information hiding).
Asynchronous message passing over shared memory - do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating.
Isolated failure handling: a failing actor is restarted or stopped by a supervision policy, not patched through shared error state.
Let it crash: design actors to fail fast on unexpected conditions and rely on supervision for recovery; defensive programming inside actors masks errors and pollutes the supervision hierarchy.
Explicit overflow policy: every mailbox needs a bounded capacity and a deliberate overflow behavior (block, drop, fail) — the pattern does not choose for you.
best_practices: Bound every mailbox and choose the full policy deliberately (block/backpressure, drop-newest, drop-oldest, drop-write); monitor mailbox depth as the saturation signal.
Never block inside a handler: offload blocking I/O to a dedicated dispatcher, thread or pool, and put a timeout on every ask.
Send immutable values and treat the message set as the actor's published protocol (sealed, enum or union types with exhaustive handling).
Keep handlers short and state transitions local; express the next behavior explicitly (Akka behavior return, Erlang state and loop, actor class with a receive loop) instead of shared flags.
Give callers a stable reference or address, never the actor instance; keep self-references and mutable internals inside.
Design the lifecycle explicitly: spawn and stop paths, mailbox draining on shutdown, dead-letter handling, and persistence when state must survive restarts.
Use supervision trees with idempotent effects: treat redelivery as normal, because delivery guarantees come from the design, not from the pattern.

Apply the 'let it crash' philosophy: prefer fail-fast termination and restart over defensive error handling for unexpected internal errors; design actors to die cleanly and restart without corrupting other actors.
Configure supervision restart intensity limits (max restart intensity and period) to prevent restart storms where a crashing actor causes its entire subtree to terminate.
Include correlation IDs in message headers for distributed request tracing across actor boundaries; propagate request context through the call chain.
Offload CPU-intensive or blocking operations to dedicated thread pools or dispatchers, keeping the actor's mailbox responsive for other messages.
Test actors by sending messages and asserting on replies using TestKit-style probes; verify behavior through message sequences, not direct state inspection.
sources: Hewitt, Bishop & Steiger, A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 1973) - origin of the actor model; Agha, Actors: A Model of Concurrent Computation in Distributed Systems (MIT Press, 1986) - actor systems, addresses, locality and composition.

related_patterns_notes.active-object: an active object owns a thread or queue and exposes asynchronous method calls; actors emphasize addressable message protocols, supervision and location transparency.
related_patterns_notes.channel-based-concurrency: channels/CSP make communication topology explicit between tasks; actors add identity, private state and lifecycle around each endpoint.
related_patterns_notes.event-based-asynchronous: event handlers react to events but need not own an addressable state machine; actors combine event handling with serialized state ownership.
related_patterns_notes.half-sync-half-async: separates asynchronous queues from a synchronous worker layer; it is an architecture decomposition, not a per-entity actor protocol.
related_patterns_notes.master-worker: a coordinator distributes jobs to workers; actors can implement the coordinator but do not imply a worker pool or job partitioning.
related_patterns_notes.structured-concurrency: scopes child tasks and joins or cancels them lexically; actors commonly outlive a call and use explicit supervision and lifecycle.
related_patterns_notes.backpressure: controls admission and rate across queues; an actor mailbox needs an explicit overflow policy but actors do not provide backpressure automatically.
related_patterns_notes.poison-pill: a shutdown-message convention; it is one lifecycle technique, not actor isolation, supervision or delivery reliability.
related_patterns_notes.proactor: completion-driven asynchronous I/O dispatches handlers for operations; an actor may own the I/O resource but is not the I/O pattern itself.
related_patterns_notes.process-manager: coordinates a distributed business transaction with compensating actions; actors may host saga steps but do not provide atomicity or compensation.
related_patterns_notes.event-sourcing: persists state transitions as an append-only log; actors can serialize commands and emit events but need event sourcing for durable history.
